new.title: Admire the Wasserturm, Mannheim's icon
new.desc: The Wasserturm was built from 1886 to 1889 to plans by Gustav Halmhuber and is 60 metres tall. It was the city's first municipal water tower and stayed on as a reserve tank until 2000. Today it is the best-known landmark of Mannheim, rising from the fountain gardens of Friedrichsplatz.
new.tip: Walk around it at dusk when the square is lit. Free, and a short walk from the main station.

new.title: Tour the vast Baroque Mannheim Palace
new.desc: Mannheim Palace was begun in 1720 for Elector Karl Philipp to plans by Jean Clemens Froimon, and is a former residence of the Electors Palatinate. The grand staircase, the Rittersaal and the Imperial Quarters stand out, and the university has used the building since 1967. The museum rooms are where a young Mozart is said to have performed in 1763.
new.tip: Check the museum hours before you go, and visit on a rainy day.

new.title: Step inside the Jesuit Church at A4
new.desc: The Jesuitenkirche was built between 1738 and 1760 in the Quadrat A4. The art historian Georg Dehio called it the most important Baroque church of south-west Germany. It is still an active parish church.
new.tip: Free entry; look at the ceiling and stucco on a bright morning.

new.title: See the shared tower of Konkordienkirche and the old town hall
new.desc: The Konkordienkirche was built between 1706 and 1717, and its tower of 1893 is the tallest in the city. It stands at the Marktplatz in G1 next to the Old Town Hall and St Sebastian church, which together form a Baroque ensemble of the early 1700s. Locals see the shared tower as a symbol of religious peace.
new.tip: Combine with a visit to the market square.

new.title: Meet at Paradeplatz and the Grupello Fountain
new.desc: Paradeplatz sits in Quadrat O1 and gets its name from the troop parades held here in the days of the Electors. In the 18th century it was called Alarmplatz. Today it is the main public transport hub of the city and features the historic Grupello Fountain.
new.tip: Use it as your starting point for exploring the grid of the Quadrate.

new.title: Stroll the Planken, the busiest shopping street
new.desc: The Planken is Mannheim's main shopping street and one of the two main axes of the Quadrate grid. Its eastern half, including the extension towards the Wasserturm, is a pedestrian zone. It is the most visited shopping street in the Rhine-Neckar metropolitan region.
new.tip: Go on a Saturday morning for the liveliest atmosphere.

new.title: Eat your way around Marktplatz and Little Istanbul
new.desc: The Marktplatz in G1 is one of the oldest and busiest squares in the city, anchored by the Old Town Hall. The area west of it is nicknamed Little Istanbul because of its many Turkish restaurants and shops. Bakeries around G1 sell fresh buns even on Sunday mornings.
new.tip: Come hungry and graze: Turkish snacks, bakery buns and Doner are all nearby.

new.title: See modern masters at the Kunsthalle
new.desc: The Kunsthalle Mannheim is a museum of modern and contemporary art on Friedrichsplatz. Its collection runs from Edouard Manet to Francis Bacon, with a focus on sculpture by Rodin, Lehmbruck, Henry Moore and others. The site combines a historic building from 1907 with a modern extension.
new.tip: Closed on Mondays; check the current exhibition before you go.

new.title: Time-travel at the Reiss-Engelhorn Museums
new.desc: The Reiss-Engelhorn Museen (rem) are a group of museums run by the city of Mannheim. The Zeughaus in C5 is one of the sites, and the Museum Weltkulturen in D5 shows a permanent world cultures exhibition. Temporary shows range from archaeology to photography.
new.tip: Closed Mondays; check which exhibition is running.

new.title: Look up at the Rosengarten beside Friedrichsplatz
new.desc: The Rosengarten, officially the m:con Congress Center Rosengarten, is a congress centre and concert hall in the inner city. Its reddish brick walls frame the Wasserturm gardens, and the colours on a sunny day are striking. Concerts and conferences are held here.
new.tip: Look at the building from the lawn side of the Wasserturm.

new.title: Hear the big organ at Christuskirche
new.desc: The Christuskirche in the Oststadt was built between 1907 and 1911 in neo-Baroque style with Art Nouveau touches. It survived the wartime destruction almost unharmed and is nearly in its original state. Its Steinmeyer organ of 1911 has about 8,000 pipes.
new.tip: Open limited hours midweek, so check before you go.

new.title: Find the neo-Gothic Lutherkirche in Neckarstadt
new.desc: The Lutherkirche was built between 1904 and 1906 in neo-Gothic style to plans by Emil During. Since 2010 it has been used as a Diakoniekirche Plus. It stands on Dammstrasse in the multicultural Neckarstadt-West.
new.tip: Pair it with a walk through the neighbourhood.

new.title: Wander the Hauptfriedhof and its Jewish cemetery
new.desc: The Hauptfriedhof is Mannheim's central burial ground, in the Wohlgelegen district. Right beside it lies the Jewish cemetery, laid out at the same time. It makes a quiet green walk away from the busy centre.
new.tip: Go on a quiet morning and keep to the paths.

new.title: Visit Marchivum, the house of city memory
new.desc: Marchivum is the city archive of Mannheim and describes itself as the house of city history and memory. It was called the Stadtarchiv until March 2018. Exhibitions tell the story of the city and its people.
new.tip: Check opening times before you go.

new.title: Check the Kunstverein, one of Germany's oldest
new.desc: The Mannheimer Kunstverein was founded in 1833 and is one of the oldest art societies in Germany, with over 700 members. The name also stands for its exhibition building on Augustaanlage. It shows contemporary art in changing exhibitions.
new.tip: Check which exhibition is on and when the building is open.

new.title: See the Popakademie on the harbour
new.desc: The Popakademie Baden-Wurttemberg is a state university for popular music and music business, founded in 2003 and based in Mannheim. It offers three bachelor and two master programmes. It is a centre of the music scene in the Jungbusch harbour quarter.
new.tip: Walk the harbour area and see what concerts are on.

new.title: Try the experiments at the Technoseum
new.desc: The Technoseum, until 2009 the Landesmuseum fur Technik und Arbeit, shows over 200 years of technical and social history of south-west Germany. There are daily demonstrations, hands-on stations and augmented reality. Experiment stations let visitors explore science and technology.
new.tip: Closed Mondays; allow half a day.

new.title: Lie back under the Planetarium dome
new.desc: The Planetarium Mannheim is the successor of a planetarium opened in 1927, one of the first in the world. Its projection dome is 20 metres high and seats 220 people. Since 2002 it has used a modern Zeiss Universarium projector.
new.tip: Book tickets ahead for weekend shows.

new.title: Roam Luisenpark and ride a gondoletta
new.desc: Luisenpark is the largest park in Mannheim, on the left bank of the Neckar in a former river loop. The lower park is the oldest part, open to the public and listed as a garden monument. Highlights include a Chinese tea house and boat trips on the gondolettas.
new.tip: Buy tickets online for a lower price and allow a full afternoon.

new.title: Marvel at the Multihalle timber grid shell
new.desc: The Multihalle in Herzogenriedpark was built for the 1975 federal garden show. Frei Otto designed the structure as a grid shell, still the largest free-form timber grid shell in the world. It is regarded as a major work of organic architecture.
new.tip: Check access and events; view it from outside any time.

new.title: Wander Herzogenriedpark and its rose garden
new.desc: Herzogenriedpark in Neckarstadt-Ost was part of the 1975 federal garden show together with Luisenpark. It has a historic rose garden, animal enclosures and the unusual Multihalle. It is a family-friendly, cheaper alternative to Luisenpark.
new.tip: Go in rose season for the garden at its best.

new.title: Spot the Fernmeldeturm from the Luisenpark
new.desc: The Fernmeldeturm is a 217.8 metre telecommunications tower built from 1973 to 1975 between Luisenpark and the Neckar. For some time it was the tallest building in Baden-Wurttemberg. It was the first tower in West Germany to use a radial beam system under its tower basket.
new.tip: Photograph it from the Luisenpark lake for a classic view.

new.title: Cycle through Spinelli Park
new.desc: Spinelli Park in Feudenheim stands on the former Spinelli Barracks of the US Army. The barracks were named in 1948 after Dominic Spinelli, an American army medic killed in April 1945 while trying to save wounded comrades. Today the area is a park, a residential quarter and a square.
new.tip: Rent a bike and go on a sunny day.

new.title: Catch a show at the Nationaltheater
new.desc: The Nationaltheater Mannheim is a four-division theatre with ensembles for opera, drama and dance, plus a young theatre. Schiller's play The Robbers had its world premiere here. It also hosts the Schillertage and the Mozartsommer.
new.tip: Student tickets are much cheaper; book ahead.

new.title: Catch a concert at the Capitol
new.desc: The Capitol is a cultural centre in a historic building that was originally built as a cinema. It hosts concerts, musicals and comedy. It is a staple of the Neckarstadt scene.
new.tip: Check the programme and book tickets online.

new.title: Join the crowd at SAP Arena
new.desc: SAP Arena is a multi-purpose hall in Mannheim with up to 15,000 seats, opened in September 2005. It hosts ice hockey, handball and big concerts. The tram stops right outside.
new.tip: Check the fixtures and concerts, and book early.
new.q: SAP Arena, An der Arena 1, Mannheim

new.title: Browse the huge Maimarkt consumer fair
new.desc: The Mannheim Maimarkt is the largest regional consumer fair in Germany. It starts on the last Saturday in April and runs for eleven days, ending on the traditional Maimarkt Tuesday. It fills the fairgrounds near the Arena.
new.tip: Go on a weekday to avoid the biggest crowds.

new.title: Arrive at Mannheim Hauptbahnhof, a rail hub
new.desc: Mannheim Hauptbahnhof handles 658 trains a day and about 118,000 travellers and visitors, making it the second busiest station in Baden-Wurttemberg after Stuttgart. It is the gateway for the Rhine-Neckar region. The palace is just next door.
new.tip: Use it as your base and walk to the palace in minutes.

new.title: Stroll Stephanienufer on the Rhine
new.desc: The Stephanienufer is the part of Mannheim's Rhine promenade in the Lindenhof district. It looks across the river to the Parkinsel in Ludwigshafen. Locals come here to walk and watch the river.
new.tip: Go in the evening for golden light.

new.title: Explore the Reissinsel nature reserve
new.desc: The Reissinsel is a nature reserve and protected floodplain forest in Mannheim. It lies on the Rhine in the south of the city. A quiet place for a woodland walk close to town.
new.tip: Stay on the paths and bring insect repellent in summer.

new.title: Watch ships from the Parkinsel beach
new.desc: The Parkinsel in Ludwigshafen is partly harbour area, partly upscale housing and partly city park. It lies on the Rhine opposite Mannheim's Stephanienufer and the Reissinsel. You can sit at the beach and watch the ships.
new.tip: Go at sunset and look across at Mannheim.

new.title: Spot the Miro wall at the Wilhelm-Hack-Museum
new.desc: The Wilhelm-Hack-Museum in Ludwigshafen is the most important museum of modern and contemporary art in Rhineland-Palatinate, with works by Malevich, Mondrian, Kandinsky, Lichtenstein and Warhol. Its landmark is the ceramic facade designed by Joan Miro in 1980. Saturdays offer free entry.
new.tip: Look at the colourful facade first, then step in.

new.title: Explore the Ernst-Bloch-Zentrum in Ludwigshafen
new.desc: The Ernst-Bloch-Zentrum was founded in November 2000 in memory of the philosopher Ernst Bloch (1885 to 1977) in his birth city of Ludwigshafen. It is housed in the historic director's villa on Walzmuhlstrasse. A small cultural and research centre.
new.tip: Check opening times before you visit.

new.title: Taste Spaghettieis, born in Mannheim
new.desc: Spaghettieis was created in the late 1960s in Mannheim by Dario Fontanella, from his father's ice cream shop. Vanilla ice cream is pressed through a spaetzle press to look like spaghetti, with strawberry sauce for tomato sauce and white chocolate for parmesan. It is a silly, delicious local original.
new.tip: Order the classic version on a warm afternoon.

new.title: Have a night at Blau in Jungbusch
new.desc: Blau is a long-running pub on Jungbuschstrasse that has been going since December 1995. Wikivoyage calls it a favourite hangout for alternative culture, and events and parties are still listed there. It anchors the Jungbusch harbour quarter's nightlife.
new.tip: Go after 8 pm, Wednesday to Saturday; check the programme.

new.title: Eat Palatinate dishes at Maffenbeier in Hemshof
new.desc: Maffenbeier is a restaurant on Rohrlachstrasse in Ludwigshafen's Hemshof district serving Palatinate dishes such as Saumagen and Winzersteak. It has a beer garden and menus in English. Hemshof blends an old German quarter with many foreign cultures.
new.tip: Try the Saumagen with a glass of local wine.

new.title: Eat pizza in a church tower at La Torre da Angelo
new.desc: La Torre da Angelo is a pizzeria in Ludwigshafen set in a former church tower. It serves traditional Italian dishes and over 50 types of pizza across multiple levels of the historic structure. High windows light the interior.
new.tip: Book ahead for evenings.
new.q: La Torre da Angelo, Maxstrasse 33, Ludwigshafen

new.title: Sip specialty coffee and cocktails at Cafe Bar Josephine
new.desc: Cafe Bar Josephine is a stylish modern cafe and bar in the heart of Ludwigshafen. By day it serves specialty coffee, in the evening a refined selection of cocktails. Wikivoyage lists it as open from late afternoon, Tuesday to Saturday.
new.tip: Pop in for an evening drink after a museum visit.

new.title: Descend into Speyer Cathedral and its crypt
new.desc: Speyer Cathedral was consecrated in 1061 and substantially rebuilt by 1106. It is the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world and one of the three Romanesque imperial cathedrals in Germany. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981 and holds the crypt of the Salian emperors.
new.tip: Visit the crypt and allow an hour inside.

new.title: Explore the Historisches Museum der Pfalz
new.desc: The Historisches Museum der Pfalz stands next to Speyer Cathedral and opened in 1910. It holds around a million exhibits and draws over 200,000 visitors a year. It counts among the most important history museums in Germany.
new.tip: Allow 2 to 3 hours; combine with the cathedral next door.
new.q: Historisches Museum der Pfalz, Domplatz 4, Speyer

new.title: Walk through a submarine at Technik Museum Speyer
new.desc: The Technik Museum Speyer has shown cars, aircraft and technical constructions since the early 1990s on 25,000 square metres of halls and 100,000 square metres outside. There is an IMAX dome theatre and a space exhibition including the Russian shuttle. You can walk through a small submarine.
new.tip: Allow a full day; a good place when it rains.

new.title: See the Altportel, one of Germany's tallest gates
new.desc: The Altportel was Speyer's western town gate and at 55 metres is one of the highest and most important town gates in Germany. It was first mentioned in 1176 and was one of 68 wall and gate towers of the free imperial city. It frames Maximilianstrasse.
new.tip: Walk from the cathedral along Maximilianstrasse.

new.title: Find the medieval Judenhof and oldest mikveh
new.desc: The Judenhof was the heart of Speyer's medieval Jewish quarter, with a synagogue built around 1100, a women's shul and the oldest surviving mikveh in central Europe. It belongs to the UNESCO SchUM sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz. The compound fell into disuse after the Jewish community was expelled after 1534.
new.tip: Check opening hours; it is a short walk from the cathedral.

new.title: Spot the Domnapf, the wine bowl of Speyer
new.desc: The Domnapf is a large sandstone bowl in front of Speyer Cathedral. According to tradition it was filled with wine for all the people after each election of a new bishop. It holds 1,580 litres and carries a Latin inscription.
new.tip: Look for it on the square as you enter the cathedral.

new.title: Look up at the Gedaechtniskirche tower in Speyer
new.desc: The Gedaechtniskirche der Protestation was built from 1893 to 1904 to commemorate the Protest at the 1529 Diet of Speyer. Its 100 metre tower is the tallest church tower in the Palatinate. It is a landmark of Protestant Speyer.
new.tip: Admire the tower from Maximilianstrasse.

new.title: Drink by the river at the Alter Hammer beer garden
new.desc: Alter Hammer is a popular restaurant and beer garden right by the river in Speyer. It sits on the Leinpfad path along the Rhine. Wikivoyage lists it as a popular spot.
new.tip: Go on a warm evening.

new.title: Try vegan Palatinate cooking at Weinstube Eulenspiegel
new.desc: Weinstube Eulenspiegel is a small wine tavern in Speyer's old town serving vegan versions of traditional Palatinate dishes. Seating is limited, so reservations are advised. It sits on Kleine Pfaffengasse near the cathedral.
new.tip: Reserve ahead; it is a tiny place.

new.title: Visit the Romanesque Worms Cathedral
new.desc: The Dom St Peter is the smallest and slimmest of the three Rhenish imperial cathedrals. It was built mainly from 1130 to 1181, after Speyer Cathedral. It no longer houses a bishop but has been a basilica minor since 1925.
new.tip: Go with time to explore the old town afterwards.

new.title: Walk Heiliger Sand, Europe's oldest Jewish cemetery
new.desc: Heiliger Sand in Worms is regarded as the oldest Jewish cemetery in Europe preserved in situ. Of about 2,500 gravestones, the oldest date from the 11th century. It is part of the UNESCO SchUM listing together with Speyer and Mainz.
new.tip: Respect the site; check opening hours.

new.title: See the Worms Synagogue and ritual bath
new.desc: The Synagogue in Worms goes back to a house of prayer founded in 1034 and has been destroyed and rebuilt several times. It is usually visited together with the old Jewish cemetery Heiliger Sand. Synagogue, ritual bath and museum are part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing since 2021.
new.tip: Check opening times and combine with Heiliger Sand.

new.title: Find the Luther Monument in Worms
new.desc: The Luther Monument in Worms was designed by Ernst Rietschel and unveiled on 25 June 1868. Together with the international Reformation monument in Geneva it is regarded as the largest Reformation monument in the world. It stands in the town where Luther faced the Diet.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk to the cathedral.

new.title: Find the only surviving Gothic church in Worms
new.desc: The Liebfrauenkirche in Worms was once a collegiate church and is today a Roman Catholic branch church. It is the only surviving Gothic church in Worms. The Liebfrauenmilch wine is named after the vineyards around it.
new.tip: Pick up a bottle of local wine nearby.

new.title: See Roman glass at the Worms city museum
new.desc: The Museum der Stadt Worms is housed in the former Andreasstift, a protected building complex with a courtyard. It covers 5,000 years of settlement around Worms from prehistoric to medieval times. Its Roman glass collection is especially impressive.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday afternoons; allow 90 minutes.
new.q: Museum der Stadt Worms im Andreasstift, Weckerlingplatz 7, Worms

new.title: Cross the Nibelungen Bridge and its tower
new.desc: The Nibelungenbruecke connects Worms across the Rhine with Lampertheim and Buerstadt and is the only road bridge between Mannheim and Mainz. It is named after the Nibelung saga and carries the Nibelungenturm, a Worms sight. The Rhine banks beyond are green and good for a walk.
new.tip: Walk across and return along the river banks.

new.title: Drink house-brewed beer at Hagenbraeu on the Rhine
new.desc: Hagenbraeu is a brewery restaurant at the Rhine promenade in Worms with views over the river. Wikivoyage recommends it for real German food with freshly brewed beer from its own brewery. Tables outside are lovely in summer.
new.tip: Sit outside by the river on a warm evening.

new.title: Stroll the park of Herrnsheim Palace
new.desc: Herrnsheim Palace is a 19th century palace in Worms's district of Herrnsheim. The surrounding park was laid out by Friedrich Ludwig Sckell, who also designed the English Garden in Munich. A quiet green stop outside the old town.
new.tip: Go in spring or autumn for a gentle walk.

new.title: Dine inside the world's largest wine barrel
new.desc: The Durkheimer Riesenfass is a barrel-shaped building in Bad Durkheim, 13.5 metres wide, with a volume of about 1.7 million litres. It is the biggest barrel in the world, but it holds a restaurant instead of wine. It stands on the western edge of the Wurstmarkt grounds.
new.tip: Order Palatinate wine and local dishes inside.

new.title: Hike to the Celtic Heidenmauer ring wall
new.desc: The Heidenmauer above Bad Durkheim is a 2.5 km long ring wall built by Celts around 500 BC. The timber parts rotted away, but the stones remain. It is a protected cultural monument in the forest.
new.tip: Wear sturdy shoes; allow a few hours for the hike.

new.title: Explore the Limburg Abbey ruins
new.desc: Kloster Limburg is a former Benedictine abbey at the edge of the Palatinate Forest. It existed from the 11th century until the Reformation and is built in Romanesque style. It counts among the largest and most important monuments of early Salian architecture.
new.tip: Walk up from town and bring a picnic.

new.title: Climb the Hardenburg castle ruins
new.desc: The Hardenburg was the seat of the Counts of Leiningen from the 13th century and got its present form in the 16th century. It was destroyed once and for all in the late 18th century. Today the ruins stand above Bad Durkheim.
new.tip: Combine with a forest walk.

new.title: Learn wine history at the Museum fur Weinkultur
new.desc: The Museum fur Weinkultur in Deidesheim shows how wine and vineyards shaped religion, art, economy, medicine and politics. It also covers the everyday life of winemakers in the past. It is housed in the historic town hall in the centre of the village.
new.tip: Stop for a tasting afterwards.

new.title: Stroll through the vineyard village of Forst
new.desc: Forst an der Weinstrasse is a small wine village in the district of Bad Durkheim and the smallest community in the Deidesheim municipal association. It has a name as a winegrowers' village. It is a short walk from Deidesheim.
new.tip: Walk over from Deidesheim and stop at a wine estate.

new.title: Hike up to the Wachtenburg ruin above Wachenheim
new.desc: The Wachtenburg is the ruin of a spur castle on a 232 metre high ridge of the Haardt, directly above Wachenheim. It looks over the vineyards to the Rhine plain. A short climb with a good view.
new.tip: Go on a clear day for the view.

new.title: Visit the Neuleiningen castle ruin
new.desc: Burg Neuleiningen is the ruin of a hilltop castle on the edge of the Palatinate Forest. It is one of three castles above the upper Eckbach valley from the early period. It sits above the wine village of the same name.
new.tip: Combine with a walk in the vineyards.

new.title: Wander Schwetzingen Palace Garden
new.desc: Schwetzingen Palace was a residence of the Electors Palatinate and was built from 1752 for Karl Theodor to plans by Nicolas de Pigage. Its highlights are the court theatre, the mosque and the palace garden. Close to Mannheim.
new.tip: Plan 2 to 3 hours; go in spring or summer.

new.title: Ride the coasters at Plopsaland Deutschland
new.desc: Plopsaland Deutschland in Hassloch opened in 1971 as Holiday Park and has belonged to the Belgian operator Plopsa of Studio 100 since November 2010. It is a large amusement park in the southern Rhineland-Palatinate. A good family day out.
new.tip: Go on weekdays to avoid queues; book online.

new.title: See Frankenthal's history at the Erkenbert Museum
new.desc: The Erkenbert-Museum in Frankenthal is a town history museum that also covers local culture and art. Its exhibits range from grave finds around 500 AD to locally made industrial products of the 20th century. Frankenthal was one of the most important places of the Electoral Palatinate from the 16th to the 18th century.
new.tip: Check opening hours before you go.

new.title: Stand where German democracy was shouted at Hambach Castle
new.desc: Hambach Castle near Neustadt, once called Kaestenburg, was a defensive site for centuries and was given its present palace-like form in modern times. It is best known for the Hambach Festival of 1832, a national democratic and unity festival, and is seen as a key symbol of German democracy. The castle sits above the vineyards of the Haardt edge.
new.tip: Go on a clear day for the views over the Rhine plain.
new.q: Hambacher Schloss, Neustadt an der Weinstrasse

new.title: See old steam locomotives at the Eisenbahnmuseum der Pfalz
new.desc: The Eisenbahnmuseum der Pfalz sits in a locomotive shed of the former Neustadt depot at the main station. The museum is protected as an important witness of railway history. It includes steam trains of the Palatine Railways and other railway machinery.
new.tip: Check opening days before you go.
new.q: Eisenbahnmuseum der Pfalz, Neustadt an der Weinstrasse

new.title: Visit Villa Boehm, the Neustadt city museum
new.desc: The Villa Boehm is a former grand bourgeois villa in Neustadt an der Weinstrasse, now listed and home to the city museum. It includes a permanent exhibition on the history of the town. A good rainy-day stop in the wine route capital.
new.tip: Check opening hours before you go.
new.q: Villa Boehm, Neustadt an der Weinstrasse
